BASE_TRAIN_SENTENCE: Training loss fell from 1.745 to 0.583, rising in only 1 of 29 epoch-to-epoch steps, and training accuracy climbed to 78.71%.
BASE_ACC_SENTENCE: Validation accuracy behaved differently: it peaked at 49.36% in epoch 22 and finished at 46.71%, so the 8 epochs after the peak bought nothing on unseen data.
BASE_TREND_SENTENCE: Validation loss reached its minimum of 0.990 at epoch 11 and then climbed 40% by epoch 30 while training loss kept falling, which is the classic signature of overfitting.
BASE_GAP_SENTENCE: The gap between training and validation accuracy widened from 3.00 pp after the first epoch to 32.00 pp by epoch 30 (78.71% versus 46.71%).
BASE_STABILITY_SENTENCE: After the first five epochs, validation accuracy moved by a typical ±1.10 pp from one epoch to the next, and its largest single-epoch drop was 1.18 pp, so optimization itself was moderately noisy; the problem with the baseline is generalization, not stability.
BS_RANK_SENTENCE: Ranked by best validation accuracy, batch size 128 came first (49.36%), followed by 512 (49.07%) and 32 (48.65%).
BS_SPREAD_SENTENCE: The gap between the best and worst setting was 0.71 pp, a difference inside the noise band that the more sensitive paired McNemar test still flags as significant (p < 0.001), so the difference is probably real but small in practical terms.
BS_EPOCH_SENTENCE: Counted in epochs, validation accuracy peaked at epoch 15 (batch 32), 22 (batch 128) and 18 (batch 512); counted in weight updates, those peaks came after roughly 21,105, 7,744 and 1,584 updates. Small batches reached their best point in fewer epochs only by taking many more steps; per update, the large batch made more progress, because each of its steps averages over 16 times as many images.
BS_LOSS_SENTENCE: The lowest validation loss was 0.996 for batch 32 (epoch 13), 0.990 for batch 128 (epoch 11) and 0.979 for batch 512 (epoch 10). By epoch 30 validation loss had risen above those minima by 40%, 40% and 41% respectively, so batch 512 overfit most strongly within the fixed epoch budget.
BS_TIME_SENTENCE: Training took 0 s at batch 32, 0 s at batch 128 and 0 s at batch 512 on this hardware (StubGPU), so batch 32 was about 1.0 times slower than batch 512 for the same 30 epochs.
BS_STABILITY_SENTENCE: Epoch-to-epoch jitter in validation accuracy (after epoch 5) was 0.99 pp at batch 32, 1.10 pp at 128 and 1.05 pp at 512, so the noisiest curve came from batch 128 and jitter did not simply track batch size in this run.
BS_SELECT_SENTENCE: I carry batch size 32 forward. Its best validation accuracy (48.65%) is within the noise band of the top score (49.36% at batch 128), and it trained 2.6 times faster, so the practical advantage outweighs a difference I cannot distinguish from noise.
BN_ACC_SENTENCE: With batch normalization, best validation accuracy went from 48.65% to 54.06% (+5.41 pp), a difference that clears both the 1-pp noise band and a paired McNemar test (p < 0.001).
BN_LOSS_SENTENCE: The lowest validation loss was 0.829 with batch normalization (epoch 9) against 0.996 without it (epoch 13).
BN_SPEED_SENTENCE: The batch-normalized network reached 46.2% validation accuracy (95% of the plain network's best) in epoch 5 (0 s), against epoch 11 (0 s) without it. After a single epoch, validation accuracy was 17.82% with batch normalization and 10.47% without.
BN_STABILITY_SENTENCE: Validation-accuracy jitter after epoch 5 was 0.84 pp with batch normalization and 0.99 pp without, and the largest single-epoch drops were 0.90 pp and 1.19 pp, so batch normalization made the validation curve smoother.
BN_GAP_SENTENCE: By epoch 30, the train–validation accuracy gap was 32.00 pp with batch normalization and 32.00 pp without, so overfitting was essentially unchanged.
BN_TIME_SENTENCE: Batch normalization changed the median epoch time by a factor of 1.04 (0.00 s versus 0.00 s), a modest overhead for the extra normalization work.
BN_VERDICT_SENTENCE: Taken together, batch normalization sped up convergence, made training more stable, and improved the best validation accuracy.
EXT_SENTENCE: At a learning rate of 0.005, the plain network's best validation accuracy was 18.65% (status: failed, jitter ±5.89 pp) and the batch-normalized network's was 55.96% (status: unstable, jitter ±5.47 pp), changes of -30.00 pp and +1.90 pp relative to the default learning rate. This fits the claim: moving to the larger step size was far worse for the plain network than for the normalized one.
RS_BEST_SENTENCE: The best random-search configuration was trial 6: 4 hidden layers of 512 units, with batch normalization, dropout 0.2, learning rate 0.0005 and batch size 128, which reached 56.65% validation accuracy at epoch 13.
RS_SPREAD_SENTENCE: Across the eight trials, best validation accuracy ranged from 47.21% to 56.65% (median 54.01%), and 4 of the eight beat the Step 4 batch-normalized reference of 54.06%.
RS_EFFECT_SENTENCE: Grouping the trials by each hyperparameter, the spread in mean best validation accuracy was largest for learning rate (8.80 pp between its best value, 0.0005, and its worst, 0.0001), followed by batch size (7.50 pp) and units per layer (6.38 pp); hidden layers mattered least (4.86 pp).
RS_UNSTABLE_SENTENCE: Of the 8 random-search trials, 2 were flagged: trial 3 (unstable; learning rate 0.005, batch size 64, dropout 0, best 47.21%); trial 8 (unstable; learning rate 0.005, batch size 32, dropout 0.4, best 54.92%).
RS_WEAK_SENTENCE: The weakest trial (#3: 4 hidden layers of 128 units, with batch normalization, dropout 0, learning rate 0.005 and batch size 64) reached only 47.21%; its key observation was: noisy validation curve (±3.9 pp per epoch).
BO_BEST_SENTENCE: The best Bayesian trial was #4 (TPE-guided): 2 hidden layers of 512 units, with batch normalization, dropout 0.2, learning rate 0.005 and batch size 128, reaching 61.11% at epoch 14.
BO_PHASE_SENTENCE: The 5 TPE-guided trials averaged 56.00% against 53.41% for the 3 random warm-up trials, and 2 of them beat the best warm-up trial, so the surrogate was already steering the search toward better regions.
BO_UNSTABLE_SENTENCE: Of the 8 Bayesian trials, 2 were flagged: trial 2 (unstable; learning rate 0.005, batch size 32, dropout 0, best 56.03%); trial 4 (unstable; learning rate 0.005, batch size 128, dropout 0.2, best 61.11%).
BO_REPEAT_SENTENCE: TPE never proposed the same configuration twice.
CMP_ACC_SENTENCE: Bayesian optimization's best trial reached 61.11% against 56.65% for random search (+4.46 pp), a difference that clears both the 1-pp noise band and a paired McNemar test (p < 0.001).
CMP_TRIALS_SENTENCE: Taking a strong configuration to mean one within the 1-pp noise band of the best score found by either method (61.11%), random search never got there within its eight trials, and Bayesian optimization first got there in trial 4.
CMP_STABILITY_SENTENCE: Trial scores had a standard deviation of 3.66 pp under random search and 4.28 pp under Bayesian optimization. Random search had 0 failed and 2 unstable trials; Bayesian optimization had 0 and 2.
CMP_COMPUTE_SENTENCE: Random search used 0.0 minutes and 178 training epochs in total; Bayesian optimization used 0.0 minutes and 176 epochs. TPE's own overhead for proposing a trial is milliseconds, negligible next to training, so the difference comes almost entirely from which configurations each method chose and how soon early stopping ended them; for example, the mean batch size was 132 for random search and 136 for TPE, and smaller batches cost more time per epoch.
CMP_VERDICT_SENTENCE: Bayesian optimization found the stronger configuration under the same budget (4.46 pp ahead, p < 0.001), although a single seed per trial means this ranking could still shift on a rerun.
FINAL_CONFIG_SENTENCE: The selected model is `bayes_t4` from Step 6: 2 hidden layers of 512 units, with batch normalization, dropout 0.2, learning rate 0.005 and batch size 128, with the weights taken from epoch 14 of the 22 epochs it trained for.
FINAL_SELECTION_SENTENCE: The top validation score overall was 61.11% (`bayes_t4`). It was flagged as unstable, but no stable run came within the noise band of it, so the rule keeps it; its validation score should be read with extra caution.
FINAL_GAP_SENTENCE: Test accuracy (53.54%) was 7.57 pp below the best validation accuracy (61.11%). Some drop is expected because the validation score was used for selection, but a gap of this size also suggests that repeated selection on the same 5,000 images has overfitted the validation set to a degree.
FINAL_CLASS_SENTENCE: Per-class test accuracy ranged from 51.31% for frog to 55.42% for airplane.
FINAL_CONFUSED_SENTENCE: The most frequent confusions were ship predicted as dog (66 images), automobile predicted as horse (66 images) and frog predicted as horse (65 images).
FINAL_CALIB_SENTENCE: The expected calibration error was 0.288. On average the model was underconfident by 8.64 pp (mean confidence 44.90% against accuracy 53.54%).
SUMMARY_GAIN_SENTENCE: From the baseline's 49.36% to the final model's 61.11%, tuning changed best validation accuracy by +11.75 pp, a difference that clears both the 1-pp noise band and a paired McNemar test (p < 0.001).
SUMMARY_LEVER_SENTENCE: Of the individual stages, searching the full space (dropout, depth, width, learning rate) produced the largest single step (+7.04 pp); the steps were -0.71 pp for choosing the batch size, +5.41 pp for adding batch normalization and +7.04 pp for searching the full space (dropout, depth, width, learning rate).
SUMMARY_PEAK_SENTENCE: In 6 of the 6 fixed 30-epoch runs, validation accuracy peaked at least three epochs before training ended, and keeping the best-epoch weights instead of the last-epoch weights was worth +3.75 pp on average.
SUMMARY_RANGE_SENTENCE: Across all 21 runs that did not fail, best validation accuracy spanned only 47.21% to 61.11%.
SEED_SENTENCE: Retraining the final configuration with seeds 7, 2024 and 31337 gave best validation accuracies of 61.11%, 61.11% and 61.11%. Together with the original run, the mean is 61.11% with a standard deviation of 0.00 pp, which is smaller than the 1-pp noise band. The original run ranked first of the four, so the original result was not simply a lucky draw.
REC_CONFIG_SENTENCE: Within this search space, the evidence supports 2 hidden layers of 512 units, with batch normalization, dropout 0.2, learning rate 0.005 and batch size 128 as a sound default, and across all sixteen search trials learning rate was the hyperparameter with the widest spread in mean validation accuracy, so it is the first one I would tune more finely.
REF_BS_SENTENCE: Batch size mainly changed how training unfolded. At batch 32 the network made 1,407 updates per epoch and its validation accuracy moved by about 0.99 pp from epoch to epoch; at batch 512 it made 88 updates and moved by 1.05 pp. Best validation accuracies were 48.65%, 49.36% and 49.07% for batch sizes 32, 128 and 512.
REF_BN_SENTENCE: Batch normalization reached the convergence target sooner (epoch 5 against 11) and finished with a best validation accuracy of 54.06% against 48.65% without it.
REF_HP_SENTENCE: Pooled over both searches, learning rate produced the widest spread in mean validation accuracy (7.96 pp). Of the 16 search trials, 4 were unstable or failed, and 4 of those used a learning rate of 0.005.
REF_GEN_SENTENCE: The unregularized baseline ended its 30 epochs with a 32.00 pp gap between training and validation accuracy, while the final model's gap at its selected epoch was 13.20 pp. Across the sixteen search trials, mean best validation accuracy was 51.68% at dropout 0, 53.33% at dropout 0.2 and 56.31% at dropout 0.4.
REF_SEARCH_SENTENCE: Under the same eight-trial budget, random search's best trial reached 56.65% and Bayesian optimization's reached 61.11%, a difference that clears both the 1-pp noise band and a paired McNemar test (p < 0.001). Measured against a target of 1 pp below the overall best, random search never got there within its eight trials, and Bayesian optimization first got there in trial 4.
REF_FINAL_SENTENCE: The final model (2 hidden layers of 512 units, with batch normalization, dropout 0.2, learning rate 0.005 and batch size 128) reached 61.11% on validation and 53.54% on the test set (95% CI 52.59% to 54.46%), and across four seeds its validation accuracy averaged 61.11% (SD 0.00 pp).
REF_WHY_CLAUSE: it is the best validation result, kept because no stable alternative came within the noise band of it
